courses.title: 01. Meet an AI agent: model, tools and harness
courses.summary: Understand what a coding agent can observe, how it acts, and why convincing output still needs evidence.

lessons.title: Model, assistant and agent
paragraphs: A language model produces outputs from its supplied input. An assistant packages that model in a conversation. An agent adds a repeated loop: propose an action, let software execute it, inspect the result, and decide what to do next. The harness is the software coordinating that loop, its permissions, state and stop conditions.

In this lab the proposals come from an editable script. Reading report.txt is real within the virtual workspace, but the next proposal is authored in advance. This separation lets you inspect which behavior belongs to the harness and which would require a model.
lessons.pitfall: A tool-capable interface does not imply every possible tool is connected.

question.prompt: Who executes a proposed tool call?

options.text: The model weights contain a live filesystem
The harness dispatches a validated call
The text prediction directly changes any computer

question.explanation: A proposal is data until the application validates and dispatches it.

lessons.title: What the agent knows about you
paragraphs: The agent can use messages, explicitly supplied project information and tool results available in its current session. Training knowledge may be incomplete or outdated; it is different from reading your current file. A connected app grants specific capabilities, not universal access to your accounts.

Ask for provenance: which file, document id, timestamp or observed test supports a statement? If the agent says an invitation was sent, inspect the tool result and app state. An explanation about an action is not evidence that the action occurred.
lessons.pitfall: Do not assume a previous conversation, private account or unsaved editor is automatically visible.

question.prompt: What establishes that a file was read?

options.text: An observed read result for that file
A confident sentence about the file
The agent saying it remembers everything

question.explanation: Evidence must come from available context or observed tools.

lessons.title: Visible traces and uncertainty
paragraphs: A useful trace records requests, tool names, arguments, outcomes, approvals and final artifacts. These are observable events. They are not a transcript of a model’s private internal reasoning, and they do not expose how every parameter contributed to an answer.

In the tutorial, Step once to see a proposal followed by a tool result. Edit the final authored response to make an incorrect claim. The files and trace stay the same. This demonstrates why a completion report should be checked against artifacts and verification results.
lessons.pitfall: Treating a polished explanation as proof makes silent tool failures easy to miss.

question.prompt: Which evidence should a reviewer prioritize?

options.text: Tool results and independently checked artifacts

question.explanation: Observable evidence is reviewable and can be compared with actual state.

lessons.title: A complete task contract
paragraphs: Define the desired outcome, relevant inputs, allowed actions, constraints and acceptance evidence. For example: read the report, draft an issue in memory, and show the draft without posting it. This is more testable than “fix onboarding” because both completion and authority are explicit.

Run the preset, change the filename to missing.txt and run again. Observe the structured error, then ask how a real agent should recover: read the directory or request the missing report, without inventing the file. Stopping with an accurate explanation can be the correct outcome.
lessons.pitfall: An endless retry loop is not persistence; it can waste money while repeating the same failure.

question.prompt: What belongs in an agent task?

options.text: Outcome, constraints and evidence of completion

question.explanation: A bounded, observable task lets the harness detect completion or a useful stopping point.

steps: Step through reading report.txt and inspect the returned text.
Run the remaining fixture turns and compare the final text with the trace.
Change the filename to missing.txt and observe the tool error.
Restore it, export the trace and explain the model/harness boundary.
courses.expected: The original run reads report.txt and finishes without changing files or app issues.

acceptance: Include the edited configuration and the observed trace.
Explain one successful case and one failure or denied action.
Separate fixture evidence from behavior requiring a real model or app.

options.text: Outcome, constraints and evidence of completion

questions.explanation: A bounded, observable task lets the harness detect completion or a useful stopping point.

courses.title: 02. Work with Codex
courses.summary: Give Codex a reviewable coding task, repository instructions, useful tools and a verification loop.

lessons.title: Orient in the repository
paragraphs: Codex is an agent product with multiple working surfaces; its behavior depends on the model, tools, environment and permissions available in that session. Begin a coding task by locating the repository, reading its instructions, and finding the smallest relevant implementation and test.

In a real project, a good first request names the observed bug and an acceptance case. Ask for a patch and evidence, such as “an unverified email must never send an invitation.” The tutorial substitutes a virtual report and repository guide for a real checkout.
lessons.pitfall: Do not infer the installed client version or available tools from a screenshot of another setup.

question.prompt: What is the useful first context for a repository task?

options.text: Repository instructions and relevant code or evidence
The entire disk without a task

question.explanation: Environment-specific evidence matters more than guesses about the client.

lessons.title: AGENTS.md and scoped instructions
paragraphs: AGENTS.md communicates project working conventions to compatible agents. Keep it focused on commands, ownership, important invariants and what completion means. More specific repository guidance may apply in subdirectories; consult the client documentation for exact discovery and precedence behavior.

The lab reads a virtual AGENTS.md. Reading it adds information to the transcript, but the scripted fixture cannot interpret it into a new plan. A real model would need the relevant instructions in context, and the harness would still enforce permissions independently.
lessons.pitfall: A markdown instruction such as “stay in this directory” is not an operating-system sandbox.

question.prompt: What does AGENTS.md primarily supply?
question.explanation: Instructions guide behavior; runtime controls enforce access.

lessons.title: Small edits and verification
paragraphs: Give a coding agent a reproducible failure, let it inspect the affected code, and evaluate the patch with a relevant check. Broad rewrites make review harder when the goal is a small behavior change. Request evidence about what was tested and what remains unverified.

In the fixture, writing draft.md pauses for approval. After approval, read the file back and compare exact content. This is a small version of edit, inspect diff, run the relevant test, and report the result. A saved patch is not automatically a deployed change.
lessons.pitfall: A successful build can coexist with incorrect behavior; choose a test that distinguishes the bug from the fix.

question.prompt: Which check directly verifies a proposed edit?

options.text: Assume saving means the task passes
Read the artifact and test the changed behavior

question.explanation: Verification needs an observable behavior or artifact tied to the task.

lessons.title: Skills, MCP and handoff
paragraphs: Skills package task guidance; MCP exposes tools or data through a protocol; the harness decides how to make these available. They solve different problems and can be used together. A skill might tell an agent how to inspect a project, while an MCP server supplies the project reader.

End a session with a concise handoff: goal, actual changed files, evidence, remaining work and constraints. Keep credentials out. For VoltQuest’s existing circuit connection, follow the documented explicit context-sharing flow; it is separate from these local AI learning notebooks.
lessons.pitfall: Installing a skill does not automatically grant an app credential or make its server reachable.

question.prompt: What should a handoff preserve?

options.text: Goal, constraints, artifacts, evidence and remaining work
API keys embedded in the narrative

question.explanation: A handoff preserves actionable state with provenance.

steps: Read the virtual AGENTS.md and report.txt.
Continue until the draft.md write requests approval; inspect the exact arguments.
Approve once, then read the saved draft in the trace.
Rerun and deny the write; compare the virtual files.
courses.expected: The write waits for approval. Approving produces draft.md; denying leaves the file absent.

options.text: Goal, constraints, artifacts, evidence and remaining work

options.text: Only the local artifact is evidenced

questions.explanation: Claims must be limited to actions actually observed.

courses.title: 03. Work with Claude Code
courses.summary: Use project memory, skills and a disciplined inspect–edit–verify workflow in Claude Code.

lessons.title: Claude Code as a tool-using product
paragraphs: Claude Code combines model reasoning with tools for development tasks. The terminal is one surface; client capabilities and permission settings determine what can happen in a given session. Do not equate the Claude model family with a specific CLI configuration.

Use a concrete request: inspect the invitation report, draft a minimal change, and explain the test evidence. The lab explores the same workflow with local files, while the official documentation explains setup and supported environments for the actual product.
lessons.pitfall: Product examples are not evidence that a feature is enabled in your current installation.

question.prompt: What determines an available workflow?

options.text: The client, connected tools and session permissions

question.explanation: A model needs a configured runtime to access tools.

lessons.title: CLAUDE.md and working memory
paragraphs: CLAUDE.md records project guidance for Claude Code. Memory instructions and current conversation context have different lifetimes, and client-managed memory features have their own settings. Keep enduring project rules separate from temporary troubleshooting notes.

In the preset, read CLAUDE.md and compare it with report.txt. The guide tells the worker how to operate; the report supplies task evidence. A concise handoff can retain an unresolved test failure without turning every transient observation into a permanent project rule.
lessons.pitfall: A stale instruction can mislead future sessions; review memory as project code changes.

question.prompt: Which fact belongs in durable project guidance?
question.explanation: Stable conventions are reusable; transient evidence belongs in a dated task record.

lessons.title: Skills and explicit invocation
paragraphs: A skill provides a focused workflow and supporting materials. Claude Code supports its documented skill conventions, including descriptions used for discovery and explicit invocation. Some frontmatter options are client-specific, so portability requires checking the destination client.

Edit the lab skill’s description to name issue triage, then load it. The trace shows the body entering context. This lab’s explicit load is an observable teaching mechanism; it does not reproduce Claude Code’s skill matching or run skill scripts.
lessons.pitfall: A skill that triggers on every request wastes context and may apply the wrong procedure.

question.prompt: What helps a client discover the right skill?

options.text: A specific description of the task and trigger
A vague description such as “be useful”

question.explanation: Discovery metadata should distinguish when the skill is appropriate.

lessons.title: Review permissions and results
paragraphs: Read operations, local changes and external writes deserve different policies. Inspect the exact proposed operation, target and data before granting a permission that matters. A previous successful read is not permission to post an issue or send a message.

Run the notebook until create_issue pauses. Deny it, then inspect list_issues. No new issue should appear. This teaches outcome checking: an agent can continue after a denial, but it must report the denial accurately and preserve the user’s decision.
lessons.pitfall: A tool’s “read-only” label is metadata; the implementation and credentials must enforce the intended scope.

question.prompt: What follows a denied issue creation?

options.text: Retry through another tool to bypass the decision
Keep app state unchanged and report the denial

question.explanation: A denial is an authority boundary, not an error to work around.

steps: Read CLAUDE.md and the report in the fixture.
Load the issue-brief skill and inspect its context contribution.
Inspect the proposed issue, then deny creation.
List issues and confirm the denied operation did not change state.
courses.expected: Skill instructions load once; denying creation leaves only the initial issue.

courses.title: 04. Work with Google Antigravity
courses.summary: Understand projects, artifacts, skills and supervised agent work in Google Antigravity.

lessons.title: Choose the right surface
paragraphs: Google’s current documentation distinguishes Antigravity’s desktop agent experience, IDE and CLI surfaces. The overview describes Antigravity 2.0 as a standalone application for managing agent work. Features and settings should be checked against the surface you actually use.

The transferable workflow is to set a scoped project, explain an outcome, inspect the plan and review evidence. This course’s lab is a browser fixture; it does not launch Antigravity or claim that another product’s command syntax works there.
lessons.pitfall: Do not treat an old IDE walkthrough as a complete description of every current surface.

question.prompt: Which source should settle surface-specific behavior?

options.text: The name of the model alone
The current official documentation for that surface
A guessed command copied from another CLI

question.explanation: Surface and release differences affect supported commands and workflows.

lessons.title: Artifacts make work reviewable
paragraphs: An artifact can hold a plan, implementation result or verification record. Its usefulness depends on concrete evidence: which files changed, what was checked, and what remains uncertain. A visually polished artifact does not establish that its claims are true.

The preset inspects a fictional invitation form and writes an artifact to a virtual file. Review the observed fields and button state before accepting the draft. For a real browser task, retain the relevant observation and reproduction steps so a reviewer can repeat the check.
lessons.pitfall: A screenshot alone may show appearance while missing the underlying behavior.

question.prompt: What makes a useful verification artifact?

options.text: Reproducible observations tied to an acceptance case
A success label with no checked behavior

question.explanation: Artifacts should help another person assess or repeat the result.

lessons.title: Skills and reusable workflows
paragraphs: Antigravity supports skill folders with SKILL.md and supporting materials. Its current documentation describes discovery metadata and loading instructions when relevant. Check the current skill locations and client-specific configuration before installation; shared skill concepts do not guarantee identical paths across products.

Build one portable workflow: gather the report, cite evidence, draft the issue, and verify any approved write. Keep optional client configuration outside the core explanation, and test the skill on both matching and nonmatching tasks.
lessons.pitfall: Copying a skill directory is only one part of portability; tools and permissions may differ.

question.prompt: What should a portable skill make explicit?

options.text: An assumption that every client exposes identical tools
Its trigger, procedure, tool needs and evidence

question.explanation: Explicit dependencies expose portability failures before execution.

lessons.title: Background work and review
paragraphs: Current Antigravity documentation includes subagents and background execution. Independent sessions need a specific task, sufficient context and bounded tools. A parent cannot assume a worker inherited every conversation detail, nor that a completed status proves correctness.

The tutorial uses a saved artifact as a small handoff. Read it back and identify which statements come from the page fixture. Later courses model task decomposition and durable state without pretending to run vendor subagents inside VoltQuest.
lessons.pitfall: Parallel execution adds coordination and token costs even when wall time improves.

question.prompt: What should accompany delegated work?

options.text: A bounded task, needed context and acceptance evidence

question.explanation: Workers need enough context and limited authority to produce reviewable output.

Review the artifact write and approve it.
Read the resulting artifact.md and compare it with the observation.
Change the artifact to include an unsupported claim and explain why it is not verified.

courses.title: 05. Write instructions and useful questions
courses.summary: Turn vague requests into scoped tasks, distinguish trusted instructions from data, and ask only useful questions.

lessons.title: Outcome before implementation
paragraphs: A task should identify a desired observable change, relevant input and what counts as finished. For an invitation bug, specify that an unverified email must not send an invitation and ask for a reproducible check. Leave routine implementation choices to the agent when you have no preference.

Compare “improve everything” with “read this report and draft a testable issue without posting.” The second gives the agent both a target and a boundary. A useful prompt can be short because it eliminates ambiguity rather than repeating generic quality words.
lessons.pitfall: Overprescribing every step can block a better implementation without making the outcome clearer.

question.prompt: Which request is easiest to verify?

options.text: Draft an issue with reproduction steps from this report

question.explanation: A concrete artifact and evidence make completion observable.

lessons.title: Authority and untrusted text
paragraphs: Instructions from the user and application establish authority; retrieved documents, webpages and tool outputs supply task data. A document may contain imperative sentences, but those sentences do not grant permissions. Models can still confuse these boundaries, so tool enforcement remains essential.

Search for the untrusted note in the fixture. Its instruction to send secrets is displayed as text. The harness has no external sending tool. A production design must likewise avoid treating retrieved instructions as a reason to expand access or bypass approval.
lessons.pitfall: Wrapping untrusted text in quotes helps labeling but is not a complete prompt-injection defense.

question.prompt: What is a hostile instruction inside a retrieved page?

options.text: Untrusted content, not new user authorization

question.explanation: Authority comes from the application and user, not from retrieved prose.

lessons.title: Ask a blocking question
paragraphs: Ask when a missing detail changes a consequential action: which repository, which recipient, or whether to publish. Give concise choices and explain the tradeoff. Continue independent read-only work when possible, but do not interpret elapsed time as consent.

The ask turn pauses until you enter an answer. It costs one modeled request when proposed; submitting an answer does not charge that same request again. A real model would use the answer to choose its next action; the scripted preset needs you to edit subsequent proposals yourself.
lessons.pitfall: A scripted sequence cannot dynamically reinterpret a user answer as model reasoning.

question.prompt: When is a clarifying question useful?

options.text: When missing information changes a consequential decision

question.explanation: Ask about missing authority or material ambiguity, not routine work.

lessons.title: Report the evidence and limits
paragraphs: An effective completion report names the artifact, the relevant checks and any unresolved limitation. It should distinguish observed results, assumptions and suggested next steps. The user should not need to reconstruct the whole trace to learn what happened.

After answering the fixture question, inspect its authored final response. Edit it into a report that cites the report.txt observation and explicitly says whether anything was created. This practices evidence-based communication without needing an LLM to generate prose.
lessons.pitfall: Do not claim a pending action happened just because it appears in the plan.

question.prompt: What should a completion report distinguish?

options.text: Observed results, assumptions and remaining work
Private reasoning invented after the fact

question.explanation: Clear evidence and limits let the user assess the result.

steps: Run until the harness asks which artifact you want.
Submit an answer and inspect the user_answer trace entry.
Observe that later proposals remain scripted rather than adapting automatically.
Edit the final turn to report only evidenced actions and run again.
courses.expected: The run pauses for a real learner answer and resumes the same ledger without duplicate charges.

courses.title: 06. Context engineering and compaction
courses.summary: Select useful context, retain essential constraints, and create handoffs that survive long tasks.

lessons.title: Working set, not an archive
paragraphs: Context is the material available for a model request: instructions, messages, tool definitions, selected files and tool results. A large context window does not guarantee every detail will be used correctly. Prefer a working set tied to the next decision, with references to larger source material.

For an invitation task, preserve the goal, the report and the permission boundary. Retrieve other documents when needed. The lab measures every selected item and the tool directory, making the overhead visible before a modeled request starts.
lessons.pitfall: Dumping an entire repository can crowd out the precise evidence needed for the next action.

question.prompt: Which context should be prioritized?

options.text: The goal, constraints and evidence for the next decision

question.explanation: A focused working set helps preserve the facts that control the task.

lessons.title: Compaction preserves meaning imperfectly
paragraphs: Compaction replaces detailed history with a shorter representation. It saves space but may lose exact values, unresolved questions or provenance. A good summary names the goal, decisions, current artifact, remaining work and constraints; important source references should remain available for rereading.

The fixture compact turn replaces unpinned items with your authored summary and retains pinned facts. No model generates this summary. Deliberately remove the email-verification requirement from the summary, then explain why pinning or rereading that rule matters.
lessons.pitfall: A compacted summary is not an exact backup of the full conversation.

question.prompt: Which fact must survive compaction?

options.text: An unresolved constraint affecting the next action

question.explanation: Losing a constraint can make subsequent actions incorrect even if the summary sounds coherent.

lessons.title: Pin carefully and leave headroom
paragraphs: Pinned material should be small and necessary. Retaining everything as pinned defeats compaction and can prevent the next request from fitting. Reserve room for the model’s output and for tool results likely to arrive before the following turn.

The sandbox checks context plus outputReserve against contextWindow before each proposal. If it already exceeds the limit, even a compact proposal cannot run; reduce the input first. This mirrors the need to compact before the context is completely full, while actual provider accounting differs.
lessons.pitfall: Cached input still occupies context; a billing discount does not create additional window space.

question.prompt: What must fit in a context window?

options.text: Input context plus the required output headroom

question.explanation: Caching affects billing, not the amount of context the model receives.

lessons.title: Handoffs with provenance
paragraphs: A handoff is a compact state record for another session or worker. Include exact filenames or document ids, the observed failure, checks performed, pending decisions and a next action. Keep uncertain assumptions labeled and exclude secrets.

Save a notebook and reload it. The editable inputs survive, while the trace is intentionally cleared so imported claims do not become evidence. A real durable system may persist trusted execution records separately; it should authenticate and reconcile those records before resuming effects.
lessons.pitfall: A copied “all tests passed” sentence is not a newly executed test result.

question.prompt: What should imported experiment evidence do here?
question.explanation: Notebook content is editable and therefore cannot establish trusted execution evidence.

Lower the context window to trigger a pre-request stop.

courses.title: 07. Tokens, windows and output budgets
courses.summary: Measure input, cached input and output separately, and understand why characters are only an estimate.

lessons.title: Tokens depend on the tokenizer
paragraphs: Models operate on tokenized input. Tokens are not uniformly equal to words or characters; code, whitespace, language and images can have different accounting. Use the provider’s tokenizer or returned usage for production measurements.

This browser deliberately uses UTF-8 bytes divided by four, rounded up. It is a visible teaching approximation, not an exact tokenizer or a billing estimate. Paste Indonesian or emoji into context and compare the estimate with the character length to see why “one word equals one token” is unreliable.
lessons.pitfall: Do not apply a fixed characters-per-token ratio as an exact limit for every model.

question.prompt: What does this lab’s byte/4 count represent?

options.text: The exact tokenizer for every provider

question.explanation: Provider tokenization varies; the lab makes its approximation explicit.

lessons.title: Count all repeated input
paragraphs: A repeated request can include instructions, tool schemas, selected context and prior results. Even a short user message may cause substantial input usage. Larger tool catalogs and verbose tool outputs can add repeated cost across a long loop.

The ledger records input for each scripted proposal. Run a read operation and observe that its result contributes to later context. Reducing a tool result to the relevant passage can lower future input, provided the omitted information is not necessary for the task.
lessons.pitfall: Counting only the newest user message misses most of an agent request’s context.

question.prompt: Which item can add input tokens?

options.text: Tool definitions and previous tool results

question.explanation: The request working set includes application instructions and tools as well as messages.

lessons.title: Reserve output before starting
paragraphs: Output limits bound a single response, while a context window bounds the combined request and response capacity according to provider rules. A tool-heavy response still needs output space. Set enough headroom for structured arguments or a useful answer without allowing unbounded text.

In the fixture, a proposed turn longer than outputReserve stops before charging. Change a short final turn into a large issue body and compare. In a real API, a response may truncate instead; your application must detect incomplete output before dispatching a partial tool call.
lessons.pitfall: A truncated JSON object must not be repaired by guessing arguments for a consequential tool.

lessons.title: Turn budgets and termination
paragraphs: Token limits, turn limits and task completion are different controls. A model can spend many small calls without finishing. Limit total turns, detect repeated failures, and stop with a clear reason when the task cannot progress. Track the partial artifact so work remains recoverable.

Set maxTurns to one while leaving multiple proposals. The first call executes; the next is stopped without another charge. A real agent should explain the remaining work rather than claim completion just because the output stream ended.
lessons.pitfall: An API finishing a response does not mean the user’s entire task is complete.

courses.title: 08. Cost management and model routing
courses.summary: Build a transparent ledger, reserve spending before requests, and evaluate quality per completed task.

lessons.title: Calculate input and output separately
paragraphs: Providers can charge different rates for uncached input, cached input and output, plus tool-specific charges. A useful ledger records quantities and rates explicitly, with the pricing source and date outside this fictional experiment. Subscriptions and API billing are separate arrangements.

The lab uses hypothetical rates per million tokens. With 1,000 input tokens, 400 cached, 200 output and rates 2, 0.5 and 8, the token cost is (600×2 + 400×0.5 + 200×8)/1,000,000 = $0.003. Do not add cached tokens twice.
lessons.pitfall: A low input rate can be overwhelmed by long output or repeated requests.

question.prompt: What is the example token cost?
question.explanation: Uncached input is 600; cached input is a subset of the 1,000 input tokens.

lessons.title: Reserve before spending
paragraphs: Before starting a request, estimate an upper bound from known input and the maximum output you will allow. Stop if it cannot fit in the remaining application budget. Afterward, reconcile with actual provider usage and account for tools and retries. Application estimates are not a guarantee about provider billing.

The fixture reserves outputReserve tokens before each turn and settles the smaller authored output. Set budgetUsd to zero to see a clean pre-request stop. Waiting for approval or answering a pending question does not issue another model request in this harness.
lessons.pitfall: A dashboard alert after spending is useful monitoring but not a pre-request budget gate.

options.text: Only when the final answer is shown

question.explanation: Preflight gating prevents avoidable new spend; settlement tracks actual usage afterward.

lessons.title: Caching and routing are measured strategies
paragraphs: Prompt caching can reduce repeated-prefix cost where supported. Eligibility, cache lifetime and pricing depend on the provider and model. Stable instructions may benefit from reuse, but a changed prefix or short prompt can miss the cache. Never mark tokens as actually cached merely because you expect a hit.

In this lab cachedTokens is an explicit hypothetical input. Compare cost with zero and a positive value while holding the context constant. Routing a simpler task to a cheaper model is a separate experiment requiring a quality check on representative tasks.
lessons.pitfall: The cheapest single call may fail more often and make the total task more expensive.

question.prompt: Which metric best compares routing choices?
question.explanation: Failures and retries contribute to total cost and quality.

lessons.title: Account for retries and parallel work
paragraphs: A retry may consume tokens even if a tool fails later. Parallel workers can reduce elapsed time but add overlapping context and coordination. Include every worker, retry, tool charge and abandoned request in a production ledger; use request ids to avoid counting events twice.

Duplicate create_issue calls in the fixture reuse an idempotency key and create one issue, but each model proposal still costs tokens. This separates business-effect deduplication from inference accounting. The same distinction matters when a network timeout leaves a write outcome uncertain.
lessons.pitfall: Idempotency avoids duplicate effects; it does not make the repeated inference free.

question.prompt: What does an idempotent retry avoid?

options.text: Duplicate business effects for the same key and payload

question.explanation: Inference calls and app mutations have separate accounting.

courses.title: 09. Design tools and validate every call
courses.summary: Build narrow tool contracts with schemas, permissions, useful errors and bounded results.

lessons.title: A tool is an API contract
paragraphs: A tool definition names an operation, explains when to use it and describes valid arguments. The model proposes values; application code validates and dispatches them. A narrow tool such as read_report is easier to control than a generic execute_anything tool.

Inspect the lab directory: each tool has exact fields and a required scope. read_file accepts one simple virtual filename. Adding an unexpected field or a path with directories produces a tool_error. This is real validation, even though the files are fictional.
lessons.pitfall: A schema shown to the model does not replace validation at the executor.

question.prompt: Where must arguments be validated?
question.explanation: The executor must treat model output as untrusted input.

lessons.title: Least authority and bounded output
paragraphs: Separate read and write permissions and grant only what the task needs. Bound input sizes, result sizes and the number of returned records. Large or sensitive results can consume context, leak information or amplify prompt injection. Return a clear truncation marker when data is omitted.

The fixture’s search returns at most three passages. The CLI companion’s GitHub reader limits fetched issues and returns selected fields. The model never receives an entire credential or an unrestricted application client.
lessons.pitfall: Giving a tool a read-only description cannot restrict a broadly privileged credential by itself.

question.explanation: Narrow targets and explicit limits reduce the exposed capability.

lessons.title: Useful errors and recovery
paragraphs: An error should identify what failed without leaking secrets or pretending success. Distinguish invalid arguments, denied permissions, missing data and transient failures. Retry only when the failure class permits it, and use bounded attempts.

Change read_file to a missing filename, then remove its read scope. The trace should show different errors. A real model can use these observations to choose a valid recovery, but the dispatcher must never expand its own authority merely to make the error disappear.
lessons.pitfall: Blindly retrying a malformed request wastes tokens without changing its likelihood of success.

question.explanation: A deterministic validation failure needs corrected input, not repetition.

lessons.title: Tool-call identity and final output
paragraphs: A real provider may return several function calls with distinct ids. Preserve each id when returning its result so the model can associate observations with requests. Handle unknown tool names explicitly. A final text response is a separate event from a successful tool execution.

The CLI capstone demonstrates a Responses function-call loop with function_call_output items. The browser trace uses numbered turns for teaching and labels its final prose as authored. In both cases, artifact inspection is the way to verify the claimed outcome.
lessons.pitfall: Do not pair a result with the wrong call id or execute a function by looking it up on a global object.

options.text: By evaluating the model’s function name as code

question.explanation: An allowlist constrains the executable capability and makes unknown names rejectable.

courses.title: 10. Discover, use and evaluate skills
courses.summary: Choose a relevant skill, load its instructions only when needed, and check its dependencies and results.

lessons.title: Skills package procedural knowledge
paragraphs: A skill is a reusable package of instructions and optional supporting resources for a particular kind of work. Its discovery metadata helps the agent choose it, while the body explains the procedure. It does not retrain the underlying model or automatically grant tools.

The issue-brief skill teaches evidence collection, drafting and verification. Load it in the fixture and inspect the additional pinned context. The actual workflow is still enforced by tool permissions and approvals, so a skill cannot bypass a denied issue write.
lessons.pitfall: A skill is not a new model weight file or a universal permission grant.

question.prompt: What does a skill primarily provide?

options.text: Reusable task instructions and supporting resources

question.explanation: Skills package procedural context; tools and credentials remain separate.

lessons.title: Progressive disclosure
paragraphs: Loading every full skill body on every request wastes context and can introduce conflicting instructions. Start with names and concise descriptions, load the relevant body, then fetch supporting references only when needed. This pattern is commonly called progressive disclosure.

Compare the context estimate before and after load_skill. A second load does not append the same body again in the fixture. That is a simple implementation choice you can reproduce in your own harness with a loaded-skill set and versioned metadata.
lessons.pitfall: A long description that contains the entire manual defeats selective loading.

question.prompt: What should discovery normally expose first?
question.explanation: Discovery should be lightweight and selective.

lessons.title: Inspect dependencies before use
paragraphs: Check the required tools, scripts, runtime, network destinations and credentials. Read installation and execution guidance from trusted sources. A skill may contain executable scripts, so reviewing prose alone is insufficient when it asks the harness to run code.

This lab never executes skill scripts; lint_skill checks a small text format only. A successful lint result does not certify that a real skill is safe, useful or compatible. For an actual installation, inspect referenced resources and test in an appropriately isolated environment.
lessons.pitfall: A syntactically valid SKILL.md can still contain dangerous or incorrect instructions.

question.prompt: What does a successful format check prove?

options.text: That the skill solves all matching tasks

question.explanation: Syntax and behavior require different evaluations.

lessons.title: Evaluate matching and nonmatching tasks
paragraphs: Test a skill on representative requests it should handle and near-miss requests it should ignore. Verify that the resulting artifact meets requirements and that tool use stays within scope. Measure extra context and tool cost, not just whether the skill was loaded.

Change the issue skill’s description to say it handles every task. Explain why a search-only question should not need its write procedure. Since the lab does not perform semantic discovery, record your match decisions explicitly in notes rather than treating a fixture load as a discovery benchmark.
lessons.pitfall: Counting activations alone rewards a skill that triggers too often.

question.prompt: What belongs in a skill evaluation?

options.text: Positive tasks, negative tasks and artifact checks

question.explanation: Trigger precision and outcome quality both matter.

courses.title: 11. Create your own SKILL.md
courses.summary: Author a focused skill with clear triggers, repeatable steps, examples and a testable outcome.

lessons.title: Start with a repeatable task
paragraphs: Choose a task whose procedure you can explain and evaluate. Issue triage is a good example: collect evidence, draft a title and reproduction steps, request approval for posting, and verify the returned issue. A skill should reduce repeated explanation without hiding important decisions.

Write down two requests that should use your skill and two that should not. “Help with code” is too broad; “turn a supplied bug report into an evidence-linked issue draft” gives discovery a useful boundary and establishes the expected artifact.
lessons.pitfall: A skill covering unrelated jobs becomes hard to trigger and harder to test.

options.text: One repeatable task with a verifiable artifact

question.explanation: Focused skills have clearer triggers and acceptance cases.

lessons.title: Write frontmatter and procedure
paragraphs: A SKILL.md begins with metadata, followed by instructions. The shared Agent Skills specification describes name and description constraints; clients can add their own fields. Use a concise, specific description and keep operational steps in the body.

The editor’s sample uses unquoted single-line name and description values. The teaching linter supports that subset, not arbitrary YAML. Try an uppercase name, fix it to issue-brief, then add a procedure that cites a document id and verifies the final issue title.
lessons.pitfall: Client-specific frontmatter should be documented instead of assumed portable.

question.prompt: Where should the detailed procedure go?
question.explanation: Metadata enables discovery; the body explains execution.

lessons.title: Supporting files and executable helpers
paragraphs: Keep long references, templates and scripts in separate files and explain when to use them. Resolve references relative to the skill’s location where the host supports that convention. Scripts should have narrow inputs, documented effects and clear failure behavior.

This browser exports SKILL.md as text and never runs referenced scripts. For a real helper, prefer a deterministic report formatter over a command that can execute arbitrary model-generated code. Test the helper independently, including malformed inputs and missing dependencies.
lessons.pitfall: A markdown link to a helper is not evidence that the helper exists or behaves safely.

options.text: Silent network access with all credentials

question.explanation: A bounded helper is easier to review and verify.

lessons.title: Version and test the workflow
paragraphs: Keep the skill with version-controlled project material or a reviewed distribution mechanism. Test trigger selection, instruction clarity, output quality and permission handling. Record which client and tool configuration you tested because portability depends on the host.

Download your edited SKILL.md, then run the lab with a denied issue scope. The skill text must not change the permission result. Add a negative task to the skill’s evaluation notes and define what a successful refusal to activate would look like.
lessons.pitfall: More instructions are not automatically better; remove rules that conflict or add no observable value.

question.prompt: What should a skill release record include?

options.text: Version, tested tasks, client assumptions and known limits
A promise to work with all tools

question.explanation: Versioned evidence makes later regressions easier to identify.

courses.title: 12. MCP: hosts, clients, servers and messages
courses.summary: Explore tool discovery, resources and prompts through an editable, versioned protocol conversation.

lessons.title: Roles and protocol layers
paragraphs: An MCP host is the application coordinating the user and model. A client connects that host to a server exposing capabilities. MCP defines structured exchanges for tools, resources, prompts and related operations; the transport carries those exchanges. It is not a model or a replacement for application permissions.

The browser fixture is an in-memory server, not a socket connection. It pins protocol version 2025-11-25 for its initialization exercise. Current specifications can change discovery and lifecycle details, so real integrations must use the negotiated version and matching SDK documentation.
lessons.pitfall: Do not copy a lifecycle sequence from one protocol version and claim it applies to every version.

question.prompt: What does MCP standardize?
question.explanation: MCP is a protocol boundary with versioned behavior.

lessons.title: Initialize, discover and call
paragraphs: For this pinned fixture, send initialize with protocolVersion, then notifications/initialized, then tools/list. Inspect the returned input schema before tools/call. Matching request ids pair responses with requests; notifications do not receive ordinary JSON-RPC responses.

Try tools/list before initialization and inspect the protocol error. Then run the correct sequence and search for onboarding. The result is a text content block containing fictional search data. This demonstrates protocol mechanics while the same application policy still controls whether the MCP tool is available.
lessons.pitfall: A reachable server can still reject a request because lifecycle or schema requirements are unmet.

options.text: A credential printed to the trace

question.explanation: The version-pinned lifecycle must be completed before feature calls.

lessons.title: Tools, resources and prompts
paragraphs: Tools perform operations with arguments; resources expose addressable context; prompts expose reusable message templates a host can present to a user. Their distinct roles help clients decide how to discover and use server capabilities. A tool description is not a trustworthy permission boundary.

Add resources/list and resources/read for handbook://onboarding to the preset. Add prompts/list and prompts/get for triage. Compare the response shapes with tools/call. The app presents all content as text and never executes an instruction merely because it came from the server.
lessons.pitfall: A server-supplied prompt still needs the host’s normal authority and trust handling.

question.explanation: Resources identify context with URIs; tools represent callable operations.

lessons.title: Transport, authentication and versioning
paragraphs: Local stdio and remote HTTP transports have different setup and trust considerations. A local server process inherits some environment and host access; a remote service needs appropriate authentication, authorization and transport protection. Use SDKs matching the server’s protocol and capabilities.

This lab supplies neither an HTTP connection nor OAuth. Its mcp:read scope grants only the fictional server tool. To connect a real app, inspect the official server’s authentication flow, requested scopes, supported version and data-handling behavior before exposing it to an agent.
lessons.pitfall: An MCP connection does not automatically make all returned content trustworthy.

courses.title: 13. Connect agents to other apps
courses.summary: Design scoped app adapters, handle identity and permissions, and verify writes without duplicates.

lessons.title: Choose a narrow app action
paragraphs: Start from a user outcome and expose the smallest useful application operation. Reading issue titles in one repository requires much less authority than administering the organization. A connector or MCP server is an adapter; the destination app still owns its data and permission model.

The local tracker has list_issues and create_issue. They require separate scopes, and creation pauses for exact approval. Inspect the title, body and idempotency key before allowing the write. The resulting issue is visible in the app-state panel.
lessons.pitfall: A general integration being connected is not permission to perform every action it supports.

options.text: All apps with a shared token
Read access to the configured repository

question.explanation: Match the credential and tool capability to the actual task.

lessons.title: Credentials belong outside model context
paragraphs: Keep secrets in environment variables, secret stores or the connector’s authentication layer. The model should receive only the capability and necessary business data. OAuth can authorize an app with scoped grants; API tokens are another mechanism whose handling and lifecycle depend on the service.

The downloadable CLI reads keys from your terminal environment. The browser notebook has no credential fields. Do not paste keys into its JSON or notes because those fields are saved and exported as ordinary user content.
lessons.pitfall: Redacting a secret from a final answer is too late if it was already sent as model input.

question.prompt: Where should an API key be held?

options.text: In the runtime’s credential layer, outside model-visible content

question.explanation: The application uses credentials to authenticate tools without exposing them as task text.

lessons.title: Read, propose, approve, verify
paragraphs: A useful write workflow gathers the current state, prepares an exact proposed operation, obtains required authorization, performs the action once and verifies the returned record. Show the destination and payload before approval. Changing the payload requires reconsidering the approval.

Deny a fixture issue creation and list issues afterward. Then start a fresh run, approve it and compare the resulting id and title. Approval is bound to the pending operation; editing the notebook clears the run, preventing an old approval from authorizing a new payload.
lessons.pitfall: A read tool succeeding does not imply a later write is authorized or has succeeded.

question.prompt: What must a write approval identify?
question.explanation: Reviewable, specific approval prevents accidental changes to a different target.

lessons.title: Idempotency and uncertain outcomes
paragraphs: A network timeout can happen after an app applied a write but before the client received confirmation. Retrying blindly may duplicate records. Where supported, use idempotency keys and reconcile with the app before retrying; otherwise design an explicit duplicate-detection or review path.

The fictional tracker remembers keys within one run. Repeating the same key and payload returns the prior issue; changing the payload with that key fails. A fresh browser run resets the fixture, so this is not a claim about durable cross-session idempotency in real apps.
lessons.pitfall: Never describe a timeout as proof that a write did not occur.

question.prompt: What can a timeout leave uncertain?

options.text: Whether the remote side effect already happened
Only the font in the response

question.explanation: Transport failure and application effect can occur at different moments.

courses.title: 14. Harnesses, sandboxes and prompt-injection defenses
courses.summary: Separate model suggestions from enforced permissions and test whether the executor can contain bad proposals.

lessons.title: The harness owns execution
paragraphs: The harness assembles context, calls a model, validates output, dispatches tools, appends observations and decides when to stop. A powerful model can still be unsafe or unreliable when the surrounding loop accepts any requested action. Build the smallest loop you can inspect before adopting more orchestration.

In the browser, edit a proposal to call an unknown tool. The allowlisted dispatcher rejects it. This is stronger than hoping the model follows a sentence saying not to call it, because the executable capability is absent.
lessons.pitfall: A prompt is behavioral guidance, not a substitute for an execution boundary.

question.explanation: Enforcement must remain effective even when a model proposes a prohibited action.

lessons.title: Application boundaries versus OS isolation
paragraphs: A virtual filesystem can isolate a teaching tool’s data because the tool never calls the host filesystem. That is different from safely executing arbitrary hostile code. Real command execution may need an OS sandbox, container or VM, with controlled mounts, identity, resource limits and network access.

The browser and offline CLI companions expose in-memory files and no shell tool. Their boundary is an application allowlist, not a certified container. If you later add code execution, reassess the threat model and test the actual isolation instead of reusing this claim.
lessons.pitfall: A process working directory is not a filesystem security boundary.

lessons.title: Treat retrieved content as hostile input
paragraphs: A webpage, issue comment or tool result may contain text designed to redirect the agent. Label provenance, minimize exposed tools, validate targets and keep credentials out of context. Require approval where consequences justify it. None of these steps guarantees perfect model judgment, so defense should be layered.

Search for the untrusted-note fixture. It asks for secret exfiltration, but there is no sending capability. Test the boundary by adding a send_secret proposal: the dispatcher rejects the unknown tool regardless of the document’s wording.

lessons.title: Hooks, approval and negative tests
paragraphs: Hooks can run checks at lifecycle boundaries such as before or after a tool call. A deterministic policy check can reject invalid arguments before dispatch; an approval gate lets a human review a concrete effect. Hook code itself is privileged application code and needs review.

Run the regression suite. It tests a permitted read, missing write scope, approval pause, path rejection, MCP lifecycle and a budget stop. These negative cases demonstrate actual boundaries, but they are not an exhaustive security certification of a deployed agent.

courses.title: 15. Retrieval, memory and evidence freshness
courses.summary: Give an agent relevant knowledge without treating search results as truth or persistent memory as timeless.

lessons.title: Retrieve for a decision
paragraphs: Retrieval selects information relevant to a question. Keyword search, embeddings and hybrid methods have different tradeoffs, but all require attention to document quality and scope. The agent should know what it is trying to establish before requesting a large body of text.

Search for “verified email” in the handbook fixture and inspect the returned onboarding passage. The lab uses deterministic word matching, not embeddings or an external vector database. Its limited corpus makes it possible to verify exactly why a result appeared.
lessons.pitfall: A retrieved passage is a candidate source, not an automatic answer or permission.

options.text: Bounded lexical matching over local documents

lessons.title: Cite provenance and check freshness
paragraphs: Useful retrieved evidence includes an identifier, relevant text and a timestamp or version when freshness matters. Distinguish the source’s update date from the date you retrieved it. If two sources conflict, investigate which one is authoritative for the task rather than blending them into a confident answer.

The handbook passage carries an owner and update date. Draft an issue citing onboarding and the observed report. The fixture has no automatic freshness check; your notes should explain what would need verification against a real organization’s current policy.
lessons.pitfall: A citation to an irrelevant page does not support a claim just because the URL is official.

lessons.title: Memory has a lifecycle
paragraphs: Working context, project instructions, searchable knowledge and durable user preferences are different memory mechanisms. Store only useful, appropriate information, with a source, scope and a way to update or delete it. A preference can change; an old task result may no longer describe current app state.

The notebook saves exact drafts and notes locally. It does not create a personal memory for any commercial agent. Compare saving “user prefers drafts before posting” with saving a transient issue id: they need different expiration and verification rules.
lessons.pitfall: Persisting everything forever increases privacy and correctness problems.

lessons.title: Evaluate retrieval and answers separately
paragraphs: A retrieval system can find a relevant passage while the agent still misstates it. Measure retrieval coverage and answer support independently. Include questions with no supporting document so the system must acknowledge missing evidence rather than fabricate a citation.

Search for a topic absent from the handbook. An empty array is a valid result. A scripted final answer can still claim knowledge, exposing why your evaluator should check citations and artifact content instead of only whether the loop returned text.

courses.title: 16. Browser, computer-use and multimodal agents
courses.summary: Reason about screenshots, accessibility observations and tool actions without confusing perception with verification.

lessons.title: Observation channels have different strengths
paragraphs: A browser agent may inspect structured page elements, accessibility information or screenshots. Structured observations can reveal labels and roles; images can show layout and visual state. Both can be incomplete, stale or misleading, and neither grants authority to act.

The lab’s inspect_page returns a fixed accessibility-style object. It contains a form heading, email field and enabled button. There is no actual screenshot model or live page control here, so use the observation to practice evidence selection rather than claim visual inference.
lessons.pitfall: Seeing a button does not establish what its server-side action will do.

question.explanation: The local fixture exposes known structured data only.

lessons.title: Act, observe and recheck
paragraphs: Computer-use workflows should re-observe after actions because coordinates, labels and page state can change. Prefer stable semantic targets when available and verify the intended effect rather than assuming a click succeeded. Treat dialogs and unexpected navigation as new evidence.

Describe the sequence you would use on a real invitation form: inspect the recipient, propose sending, obtain the needed permission, submit, then confirm the destination record. The local fixture lets you record that plan as an artifact but never clicks a real application.
lessons.pitfall: A coordinate from an old screenshot may target a different control after layout changes.

question.explanation: Fresh evidence detects failed, redirected or unexpected actions.

lessons.title: Multimodal inputs still consume resources
paragraphs: Images, audio and video have provider-specific input formats, token accounting and limits. Resolution, sampling and repeated frames can affect cost and latency. Send only the relevant evidence and use current model documentation for exact pricing and supported modalities.

This lab’s byte-based text estimator does not estimate image or audio tokens. If you add multimodal support to your CLI, keep usage from provider responses in a separate typed record rather than pretending a screenshot’s character count represents its cost.

paragraphs: Browser automation can affect real people through messages, purchases, permissions and published content. Separate observation from approval for the exact side effect. Keep authentication state scoped and avoid transmitting unrelated visible information to a model.

In the tutorial, a local write records a proposed browser check and pauses for approval. That pause is a teaching analog, not proof that real browser automation is isolated. For production, test account permissions, navigation limits and the tool’s actual execution environment.

courses.title: 17. Subagents, teams and coordination
courses.summary: Split work only when tasks are independent, control shared state, and account for coordination cost.

lessons.title: Choose a decomposition with real independence
paragraphs: A subagent can focus on a bounded task with its own context and return a result. Multiple workers help when research, implementation or review can proceed independently. Dependent steps or edits to the same file can create more coordination work than they save.

Divide the invitation investigation into evidence gathering and test-design review. Give each worker an output artifact and a clear stopping condition. The lab runs scripted handoff artifacts sequentially; it illustrates interfaces without pretending to launch parallel model sessions.
lessons.pitfall: More agents do not automatically mean better quality or lower cost.

lessons.title: Context isolation and handoff contracts
paragraphs: A worker needs its goal, relevant constraints, source locations and expected output. Do not assume it sees the parent’s full history. Current products differ in context inheritance and messaging behavior; check their documented session model. A concise handoff can reduce duplication while retaining the facts that matter.

Write worker-a.md with a finding and source id, then have a reviewer read that artifact. The reviewer should receive the user’s “draft only” constraint directly, rather than infer it from an ambiguous summary.
lessons.pitfall: A worker’s missing context can cause a correct local decision that violates the overall task.

lessons.title: Shared workspace and merge conflicts
paragraphs: Separate branches or worktrees can reduce accidental file contention, but merging still requires review and tests. Shared directories need explicit ownership, coordination and awareness of concurrent changes. Parallel readers can often share data safely; parallel writers need stronger discipline.

The fixture stores two virtual artifacts and a combined review. Inspect which worker owns each artifact and which checks belong to the coordinator. A real worktree is a Git workflow convenience, not an operating-system security sandbox.
lessons.pitfall: Worktree isolation does not automatically restrict network access or host filesystem permissions.

question.explanation: Git working copies are not security sandboxes.

lessons.title: Current team features and evaluation

Claude Code’s current agent-team documentation labels that feature experimental and describes independent session contexts; Antigravity documents configurable subagents. Treat feature availability and exact setup as version-specific. Evaluate your coordination design before adopting it for high-cost work.

Measure completed-task quality, total requests and review overhead against a single-worker baseline. A successful coordinator should challenge unsupported worker claims and combine evidence, not merely concatenate confident summaries.
lessons.pitfall: Agreement between agents is not independent evidence when they share the same incorrect source.

courses.title: 18. Durable workflows, checkpoints and asynchronous tasks
courses.summary: Recover long-running work, distinguish waiting from failure, and prevent duplicate effects on resume.

lessons.title: A run needs explicit state
paragraphs: Long-running tasks benefit from a state machine: ready, waiting for a user, waiting for a tool, completed, failed or cancelled. Persist the task identity and relevant state separately from a chat summary. A response stream ending is not enough to determine whether the business task finished.

The harness exposes ready, question, approval, completed and stopped states. Step into a question, then inspect the unchanged cursor and ledger while waiting. Resuming supplies an answer to the pending turn rather than starting the entire task again.
lessons.pitfall: Treating all pauses as failures can trigger duplicate requests and writes.

lessons.title: Durability is more than saving a transcript
paragraphs: A durable workflow records enough trusted state to resume safely after interruption. It may need tool-call ids, approved payloads, idempotency keys and externally reconciled effects. Stored messages alone cannot prove whether a remote mutation happened.

The browser notebook intentionally saves editable inputs, not executable resume state. Reloading starts fresh fixtures. This keeps imported claims from authorizing actions, but it is not durable execution. Use that distinction to design what a production checkpoint would need to authenticate and validate.

lessons.title: Idempotent effects and reconciliation
paragraphs: Persist a stable operation key before performing a retryable write where the app supports it. After interruption, reconcile the key and effect rather than blindly rerunning every step. Distinguish retryable transient errors from invalid arguments and permission denials. Cancellation also needs a policy for work already in flight.

The issue fixture deduplicates within one run. Repeat the same payload and key to see replayed: true. Change the payload to expose the conflict check. A real system must keep equivalent state durably or use the destination service’s idempotency mechanism.

The CLI companion uses Responses so you can see the loop directly. It does not implement a durable workflow engine or MCP tasks. Compare the explicit state you would need to add with the responsibilities a managed runtime or workflow framework can take on.

courses.summary: Measure outcomes and boundary behavior, inspect failures, and compare changes against a fixed baseline.

lessons.title: Define observable success
paragraphs: An evaluation task needs an input, an expected outcome and a way to inspect evidence. For issue creation, verify title, content, destination and count. Include constraints such as no write without approval. A model saying “done” should not be the grader’s only signal.

The fixture regression suite checks actual files, issues and trace types. Its read test looks for invitation evidence in returned text, while its denied-write test checks that a file was not created. These tests exercise the harness rather than a model’s language quality.

lessons.title: Negative and adversarial cases
paragraphs: Cover malformed arguments, missing permissions, oversized context, exhausted budgets, absent data and hostile retrieved instructions. Negative cases check that failures remain contained and understandable. Include ordinary valid behavior so a defense does not “pass” by blocking everything.

The suite pairs a successful read with denied writes, path rejection and budget stops. Change the preset and run it again. Remember that the suite uses its own controlled cases; it does not certify every arbitrary plan you type into the editor.

lessons.title: Separate model quality from harness correctness
paragraphs: Deterministic unit tests can verify dispatch, state transitions and budgets. Model evaluations require actual model runs on representative tasks and may vary between attempts. Record model identifier, configuration, dataset version and grading method when comparing quality.

lessons.title: Add a model adapter deliberately
paragraphs: The live companion uses the OpenAI Responses API over HTTPS and requires an environment API key plus a model id you choose. It returns each function result with the provider’s call id. Every request has a timeout and output bound; the loop has a maximum number of turns.

Review the instructions shown beside the source before enabling live mode. Model availability, pricing and usage differ by account and release. The program reports returned usage; it does not infer a dollar invoice from invented rates or claim a hard account-wide spending cap.
lessons.pitfall: Never place an API key in a downloaded notebook, source-control commit or browser field.

lessons.title: Add tools and one real app reader
paragraphs: The companions implement narrow virtual file and draft tools plus an optional GitHub issue reader. GitHub access is enabled explicitly and limited to a configured owner/repository at the fixed official API host. Results include selected fields and are bounded. No GitHub write tool or arbitrary URL fetch is exposed.

Run the offline demo first, then use a read-only credential if your repository requires one. Real network access happens only from your own terminal after opt-in. The browser fixture remains independent, and its fictional issue ids are never sent to GitHub.
lessons.pitfall: An application allowlist is not an OS sandbox for arbitrary code execution.

lessons.title: Verify, extend and document limits
paragraphs: Run both companions’ self-tests and compare the same offline task. Check malformed arguments, denied writes and unknown tools before adding another adapter. For MCP, use the earlier protocol course and an official SDK matching your chosen version; the companions do not claim to include a complete MCP transport.

Your final project should include a task contract, skill, tool schema, trace, evaluation cases and a clear sandbox description. Add durable checkpoints, production credential management and provider-aware cost gates as separate tested extensions. The supplied CLI is a working teaching baseline, not a production certification.
lessons.pitfall: A passing offline test cannot prove a paid model call, vendor CLI session or authenticated external app works.
